title: 1. Origin, Corporate Evolution & Past Stock Cycles

epigraph.quote: We have been designing and building computing systems in India for more than twenty-five years. When the world finally discovered that AI needs serious hardware, we were already in the room.
epigraph.author: Sanjay Lodha, Chairman & Managing Director, Netweb Technologies, FY2026 Annual Report

web_blocks.html: Netweb Technologies India Limited was founded in 1996 as a proprietorship by Sanjay Lodha and was incorporated as a company in 1999 in Faridabad, Haryana. Its founding bet was unfashionable at the time: rather than importing finished servers and reselling them, Netweb would design, engineer and assemble high-end computing machines inside India. For its first two decades the company stayed deliberately small and highly specialised, servicing national research institutions, defence laboratories and public-sector undertakings that needed bespoke supercomputers but could not buy them off a global catalogue.

That specialisation produced a sequence of nationally visible engineering milestones. In 2004 Netweb deployed KABRU at the Institute of Mathematical Sciences, Chennai, which entered the world's Top 500 supercomputers at commissioning. In 2013 it deployed PARAM Yuva-II at C-DAC, Pune, then among the most powerful machines in the country. In 2019 it deployed PARAM Ambar for ISRO, and in 2023 it delivered AIRAWAT, which was India's largest and fastest AI supercomputer at the time of commissioning. Over its life the company has installed more than 600 supercomputing systems and placed machines in the global Top 500 list seventeen times, and it has shipped over 10,000 accelerator or GPU-based AI systems.

The corporate evolution since 2019 has been a story of stacking two durable adjacent businesses on top of that supercomputing base. The first was private cloud and hyperconverged infrastructure, launched as a commercial line around 2015 and now sold under the Skylus brand. It let enterprises and banks run their own compute and storage estates instead of renting public cloud. The second, and the one that changed the company's economics, was AI systems. Netweb qualified under the Government of India's PLI 1.0 scheme for IT hardware in 2021. It qualified under PLI 2.0 for telecom and networking products in 2022. It listed on the NSE and BSE on 27 July 2023. In November 2023 it became a manufacturing partner for NVIDIA's Grace CPU Superchip and GH200 Grace Hopper MGX server designs, committing to build more than ten server variations under its Tyrone range.

web_blocks.takeaway: Revenue compounded at roughly 50% a year for eight years, but the quality of that compounding changed shape: through FY2025 growth was funded largely by working capital, and only in FY2026 did operating cash flow (₹171 crore) finally run ahead of net profit.

web_blocks.html: The stock has lived through three distinct cycles. It listed on 27 July 2023 at ₹950 against an issue price of ₹500, a listing gain of about 89%. But the post-listing euphoria faded quickly. The shares drifted to an all-time low of ₹738.60 on 26 October 2023 as early investors exited and the market discounted a small, lumpy, project-based order book. The second cycle, spanning 2024 into 2025, was a slow re-rating. The AI narrative, the NVIDIA partnership and a visibly expanding order book pulled the stock steadily higher. The sovereign-AI order worth ₹1,734 crore, announced on 3 September 2025, was the turning point. That order, for NVIDIA Blackwell-based systems under the IndiaAI Mission, made the market treat Netweb as an AI-infrastructure proxy rather than a supercomputing integrator.

The third cycle is the one investors are living through now. The stock made an all-time high of ₹5,813 on 24 August 2026. That came days after the company completed its first equity raise since listing — a ₹1,200 crore qualified institutions placement priced at ₹4,790 per share on 20 August 2026. It then gave back a large part of that gain. Global anxiety about the durability of AI capital expenditure peaked, and the market began to scrutinise the company's rising inventory and lengthening cash-conversion cycle. By early November 2026 the share price was trading in the mid-₹4,000s, roughly 28% below the August peak, even as reported earnings were accelerating. History here is a warning against both extremes. This is a business whose operating results have compressed a decade of growth into three years, and whose share price has repeatedly swung far ahead of, and then back toward, those results.

web_blocks.title: The Pattern to Notice: Operating Leverage Arrives Late and Unevenly
paragraphs: Look at the shape of the two series in Table 1.1. Revenue multiplied nearly seventeen-fold from FY2019 to FY2026, but operating margin did not expand in a straight line — it climbed from 5% to 16% between FY2019 and FY2023, then settled back to 13% as the mix shifted toward very large, lower-margin AI systems deals. This is the signature of a systems integrator, not a software compounder: each new growth engine arrives with a different gross-margin profile, and the overhead base is shared across all of them.

That is precisely why the cash-flow line matters more than the profit line in this company's history. Netweb reported profits every year, but between FY2021 and FY2025 it converted a cumulative operating profit into negative free cash flow, because executing large orders meant buying expensive components — GPUs, memory, switches — long before customers paid. Only FY2026, when customer advances and faster collections arrived alongside the orders, turned the cash engine positive. Any future AI downcycle would first show itself in exactly this line.

web_blocks.html: Two structural pivots define where the company stands today. The first is the shift from a domestic research-and-defence installer to a commercial OEM with a full-stack portfolio. That portfolio now spans AI systems, HPC, private cloud and HCI, high-performance storage, data-centre servers and software/services, sold under the Tyrone and Skylus brands. The second is the geographic and balance-sheet pivot underway in 2026. The board approved a wholly owned R&D subsidiary in Taiwan to access hardware-design talent near the major silicon vendors' design centres. And the ₹1,200 crore QIP turned the company from net-debt-negative on operating cash to comfortably funded for a working-capital-heavy expansion. Both moves say the same thing. Management believes the AI-infrastructure window is a multi-year platform shift and is willing to finance inventory and hire ahead of it.

book_paragraphs: If you want to understand Netweb Technologies, you and I should start not in a data centre but in a modest industrial town in Haryana in the late 1990s. Sanjay Lodha had begun building computing systems as a sole proprietorship in 1996, and by 1999 he had incorporated Netweb Technologies India Limited in Faridabad. His founding decision was almost contrarian: while the rest of the Indian IT channel imported finished servers and marked them up, Lodha insisted on designing and assembling the machines himself, in India, for buyers who needed something no global catalogue offered.

For two decades that decision looked like a niche, not a platform. Netweb's customers were national research laboratories, defence establishments and public-sector undertakings — institutions that needed bespoke supercomputers and were willing to work with a local engineering house that could tune the interconnect, the cooling and the software stack to their specific workloads. Ask yourself how a company survives on that clientele for twenty years: only by being genuinely better than a box-shifter, because the customer can always buy a branded machine instead. Netweb's answer was integration depth — it did not just assemble a supercomputer, it designed the architecture, supplied the middleware, and supported the machine for its life.

That patient period produced the engineering proof points that later became the company's marketing. In 2004 it deployed KABRU at the Institute of Mathematical Sciences in Chennai, a machine that entered the world's Top 500 supercomputers at commissioning. In 2013 came PARAM Yuva-II at C-DAC in Pune. In 2019 came PARAM Ambar for ISRO, and in 2023 came AIRAWAT, which was India's fastest AI supercomputer when it went live. More than 600 supercomputing systems and more than 10,000 GPU-based AI systems later, the pattern is clear: Netweb's brand was built one marquee national project at a time.

Now watch the business migrate. Around 2015 the company began selling private cloud and hyperconverged infrastructure — the Skylus line — which let banks, enterprises and government bodies run their own compute and storage estates rather than renting public cloud. This was the first stacking move: the same customer who trusted Netweb to build a supercomputer could also trust it to run their internal cloud. Then came AI systems, and with them the economics changed entirely. The company qualified for the government's PLI incentives, listed on the exchanges in July 2023, and in November 2023 signed a manufacturing partnership with NVIDIA for its Grace and Grace Hopper MGX server designs under the Tyrone brand.

Run your eye down Table 1.1 in the web edition. Revenue climbs from ₹130 crore in FY2019 to ₹2,184 crore in FY2026 — roughly a seventeen-fold increase in eight years, a compound rate near 50%. But notice where the margin line goes. Operating margin rises from 5% to 16% between FY2019 and FY2023, then slides back to 13% by FY2026. And notice the cash line even more carefully: from FY2021 through FY2025, Netweb reported profits while generating negative free cash flow, because executing a large AI order means buying GPUs, memory and switches months before the customer pays. Only in FY2026, with customer advances and faster collections, did operating cash flow of ₹171 crore finally exceed net profit of ₹206 crore. That single fact explains almost everything about how to value this company.

The stock tells its own story of extremes, and you should hold both halves of it in mind. The shares listed in July 2023 at ₹950 against a ₹500 issue price, then fell to an all-time low of ₹738.60 in October 2023 as early investors left. Through 2024 and 2025 the market slowly re-rated the business as the AI order book became visible, and the ₹1,734 crore sovereign-AI order announced in September 2025 turned Netweb into an AI-infrastructure proxy in many investors' minds. The stock peaked at ₹5,813 on 24 August 2026, just after a ₹1,200 crore qualified institutions placement was priced at ₹4,790, and then corrected sharply as global fears about the sustainability of AI spending peaked and sceptics began asking hard questions about inventory and cash conversion.

What should you take from this cycle history? First, that Netweb has repeatedly swung from euphoria to neglect and back, which means your entry discipline matters more than your thesis. Second, that the operating record is real — this is not a story stock with no earnings; the profits, revenues and marquee deployments genuinely happened. And third, that the business is a systems integrator with a chameleon's margin profile, so each time it adds a new growth engine the margin mix changes and the cash-flow pattern changes with it.

The two structural moves now underway deserve your attention. The board has approved a wholly owned R&D subsidiary in Taiwan, not to manufacture abroad but to hire hardware-design engineers near the silicon vendors' design hubs so Netweb can keep pace with NVIDIA's and AMD's release cadence. And the ₹1,200 crore QIP, the company's first equity raise since listing, has funded the working capital to chase a very large order book. Both moves are bets that the AI-infrastructure window is a multi-year platform shift. As you read the rest of this monograph, keep asking the central question that this history poses: is Netweb a durable platform that happens to look like an integrator, or an integrator that is enjoying the most favourable demand cycle of its life?

book_callouts.title: The Founder's Unfashionable Bet
book_callouts.text: Notice how many times Netweb chose the harder path. It designed rather than resold. It served research institutions that paid slowly rather than chasing easy distribution. It built in India a decade before 'Make in India' made that commercially fashionable. And when NVIDIA offered a manufacturing partnership in 2023, it committed not to one server but to more than ten variants. Each of these choices looked inefficient at the time and turned out to be the foundation of a moat — or at least of a licence to bid on work its competitors could not.
